  410 AVALON CANYON ROAD
  AGENDA

  In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this
  meeting, please contact the City Clerk’s Office (310) 510-0220. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting will
  enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. (28 CFR 35. 102-
  35.104 ADA Title II). All public records relating to an agenda item on this agenda are available for the public
  inspection at the time the records are distributed to all, or a majority of all, members of the City Council. Such
  records shall be available at City Hall located at 410 Avalon Canyon Rd.

For the public’s convenience, but not participation, the meeting can be viewed:
  On local cable: Catalina Broadband Solutions channel 3
  Streaming on Facebook Live: www.facebook.com/CityOfAvalonOfficial
  Streaming on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/CityofAvalonCA

ORAL COMMUNICATION
Members of the public may address the City Council at this time. No action will be taken on non-
agenda items at this meeting. Speakers should limit comments to two (2) minutes each.

PRESENTATION  Robert Greenlaw will provide a presentation regarding findings from the
  —

Elbow Demo at the intersection of Pebbly Beach Road and Crescent Avenue, and discuss next
steps as we move toward the next visitor season.

CONSENT CALENDAR

1.  City Council Minutes
  Although the live recording is the official record of public meetings, minutes are prepared
  for the Council’s approval.
  Recommended Action
  Approve minutes from the October 1, 2024 regular City Council Meetings.

2.  Warrants
  Expenditures Submitted for Approval
  o Warrants from the US General Fund in the amount of $1,485,869.77.
  o One payroll totaling $264,772.82.
  o Three electronic fund transfers totaling $95,062.52.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
OCTOBER 22, 2024
PAGE 2

  Recommended Action
  Approve total expenditures for September 23, 2024 through October 4, 2024 totaling
  $1,845,705.11.

3.  Fiscal Year 2024-2025 First Quarter Treasurer’s Report
  State and Municipal Codes require the Treasurer to submit within
  30 days following each fiscal quarter a report summarizing the City’s cash and investment
  balances. Attached is the First Quarter Treasurer’s Report for FY24-25. The report was
  shared with the City Treasurer prior to presentation to City Council.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt the resolution accepting the FY24-25 First Quarter Treasurer’s Report.

4.  Authorize the Purchase of SCBAs
  SCBAs provide respiratory protection for firefighters in fire suppression events including
  structure and brush fires. These systems must meet standards set forth by the National
  Institute of Occupational Safety and Health.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the procurement of MSA Gi Deluxe Custom Harness packs, bottles and
  accessories from for a not to exceed the sum of $400,000 as budgeted in the Fiscal Year
  2024-25 Capital Improvement Plan Project Number 244501.
  -

PUBLIC HEARING

5.  Fiscal Year 2024-2025 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule Revisions
  The City charges fees for miscellaneous public services, use of City facilities and
  equipment rental and other activities. User fees are assessed and collected for City
  services and programs provided by various departments. These are services that convey
  a benefit, grant a privilege, provide for review and enforcement of regulatory activities,
  enforce laws, or are a condition of development. Under State law, cities may charge fees
  to recoup the direct and indirect costs related to the provision of user services.
  Recommended Action
  1. Hear a presentation regarding the Miscellaneous Fee Schedule. 2. Open the Public
  Hearing to hear public comments. 3. Close the Public Hearing. 4. If consensus, adopt the
  fee schedule as proposed.

6.  Appeal of Planning Commission Action No. 24-08 of PC#2842 Approving a Site Plan,
  Conditional Use Permit, Variance and Coastal Development Permit at 301 Beacon Street
  On August 28, 2024, the Planning Commission held a duly noticed public hearing to
  consider PC#2842, a request for a Site Plan Review, Conditional Use Permit, Variance,
  and Coastal Development Permit to allow demolition of a vacant three-story apartment
  building and construction of a new four-story hotel with employee housing at 301 Beacon
  Street. On September 9, 2024, Diana Conover, owner of 310 Metropole Avenue, and
  Robert and Laurie Glaser, owners of 314 Metropole Avenue, filed a timely appeal of the
  Planning Commission’s decision, requesting that the City Council review the Planning
  Commission’s approval of the Project.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
OCTOBER 22, 2024
PAGE 3

  Recommended Action
  1. Open the Public Hearing. 2. Receive Public Comment. 3. Close the Public Hearing. 4.
  Consider the appeal and determine to either: a) Affirm the action of the Planning
  Commission; b) Require a transcript or recording of the testimony, and all other evidence
  upon which the Planning Commission made its decision, and after receiving such
  evidence take such action as, in its opinion, is indicated by such evidence alone; c) Refer
  the matter back to the Planning Commission, with or without instructions for further
  proceedings; or d) Set the matter for hearing before itself, considered de novo. (Avalon
  Municipal Code (AMC) Section 9-8.601)

GENERAL BUSINESS

7.  Coyote Joe’s Outdoor Patio Lease Assignment
  On September 23, 2024, City Staff received a request from Ron Bevins, representing
  Seabring, Inc., dba Coyote Joe’s Restaurant, to assign the remaining term of his lease
  with the City of Avalon for exterior space at 113 Catalina Avenue to Martin Leyva, dba
  Coyote Joe’s Bar and Restaurant, LLC. The exterior space, comprised of approximately
  418 square feet, is currently used for outdoor dining. Per the lease agreement, any
  assignment must be approved by the City Council.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the assignment of the lease for city-owned real property at 113 Catalina Avenue
  from Seabring Inc., dba Coyote Joe’s Restaurant to Coyote Joe’s Bar and Restaurant,
  LLC.

8.  Cabrillo Mole Rehabilitation Phase II Pre-Construction Stage 0
  The City completed Phase 1 of the Cabrillo Mole Rehabilitation Project which included
  the rehabilitation and reinforcement of the existing concrete members, replacement of the
  steel grates, and repaired the concrete deck and railing in 2020. The next portion of the
  project will replace and reconfigure the existing building and structures to improve
  passenger queuing and adjacent transportation circulation. In order to accommodate
  sustained, mostly uninterrupted operations of the Cabrillo Mole, construction of the new
  facility has been broken into 10 construction stages.
  Recommended Action
  1. Hear a presentation regarding Construction Stage 0 of Phase II of the Cabrillo Mole
  Rehabilitation Project. 2. Authorize the implementation of Stage 0 of the Cabrillo Mole
  Rehabilitation Project including approval of the Cabrillo Mole Temporary Facility Plan,
  four step procurement process, administrative procedure for existing tenants at the
  Cabrillo Mole, and approval of the site plan. 3. Make the affirmative finding that the City
  has made its best effort to relocate the tenants at the Cabrillo Mole, and suitable facilities
  for the Catalina Island Company’s ticket booth, Island Enterprises’ ticket booth and
  storage area, Catalina ATM, Inc., and Fish Feeder business cannot be accommodated.
  4. Delegate authority to the City Manager to negotiate and execute reasonable rent
  agreements with tenants that will be relocated to temporary facilities during construction
  including the Avalon Blue Line Baggage, Catalina Express, Catalina Passenger Services
  (Flyer), and Eli’s Island Deli.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
OCTOBER 22, 2024
PAGE 4

9.  Five Corner Pedestrian Improvements Project Contract Award
  The bidding deadline for contractors interested in the City’s Five Corner Pedestrian
  Improvement project was September 10, 2024 at 11 a.m. No bids were received by the
  stated deadline; however, Jordhal Construction, Inc. did submit a bid on the deadline
  date. The bid received was approximately twice the sum anticipated by the engineer’s
  estimate. Therefore, the City Council authorized the City Manager, per the City’s
  Purchasing Policy, Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.206 (e), to enter into negotiations
  with Jordhal Construction, Inc. to modify the scope of the project to align with available
  funding.
  Recommended Action
  1. Authorize the City Manager to execute a contract with Jordhal Construction, Inc. for the
  completion of the Five Corners Pedestrian Improvement Project for a base scope not
  exceed the sum of $4,737,805. 2. Authorize the City Manager to amend the construction
  contract to approve construction line items once a scope of work, to be proportionally
  reimbursed by third-party entities, is finalized for a not to exceed amount equal to a
  reimbursement agreement amount. 3. Authorize the City Manager, at his discretion, to
  amend the construction contract to approve additive items for a not to exceed sum of
  $350,000 for development items associated with a future workforce housing project.

10.  Options for City Council in Considering Tenant Protection and Rent Control Measures
  The purpose of this staff report is to provide the City Council with information on State
  law as it relates to tenant protections and rent control, and provide examples of what other
  cities have codified locally so the City Council may consider what policy options it is
  interested in exploring for Avalon.
  Recommended Action
  Consider and discuss tenant protections and rent control options available under State
  law, and provide direction to City of Avalon (‘City”) staff to evaluate and report back on
  any desired local options available to the City.

ADJOURN

NOTICE OF POSTING

I, Devin Elise Hart, declare that the City Council Agenda for Tuesday, October 22, 2024 was
posted on Friday, October 18, 2024 on the City’s website, www.cityofavalon.com/agendacenter,
and at City Hall, 410 Avalon Canyon Road.

Devin Elise Hart, Management Analyst

4.  City Manager Employment Agreement Merit Increase

  Amended the compensation terms of the Employment Agreement for City Manager
  Services with David Maistros dated December 10, 2021, providing a 5% merit increase
  to the City Manager’s base pay retroactively effective beginning on February 1, 2024.
 CITY COUNCIL MINUTES
OCTOBER ‘1, 2024
PAGE 2

GENERAL BUSINESS

5.  Discussion Regarding Tents on the Beach
  City Council heard the presentation and directed staff to amend the existing ordinance
  with the following changes to Middle Beach and South Beach only:
  -Prohibit canopies, tents, and umbrellas larger than 6 feet by 6 feet. The shade
  structures will need to be open on all sides to not obstruct the view.
  -Baby shade structures will be allowed.
  -No large folding tables.
  -No beach items are to be left on the beach overnight.
  -No beach items and personal belongings are to be left unattended.

6.  Sidewalk Vending
  City Council heard the presentation and approved the addition of two additional
  sidewalk vending locations at the intersection of Crescent Avenue and Pebbly Beach
  Road (the area known as “the elbow”):
  1) Vacant Paddle Board Stand.
  2) Adjacent to the Photo Booth.

Mayor Marshall adjourned the meeting at 7:06 p.m.

I, Gabrielle Morones, City Clerk, do hereby certify that the DVD videotape of the regular City
Council Meeting on October 1, 2024, is the official record of the Council Meeting and is on file
and maintained in City Hall.

Gabrielle Morones, City Clerk

SUBJECT:  Fiscal Year 2024-2025 Rrst Quarter Treasurer’s Report

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt the resolution accepting the FY24-25 First Quarter
Treasurer’s Report.

REPORT SUMMARY: State and Municipal Codes require the Treasurer to submit within
30 days following each fiscal quarter a report summarizing the City’s cash and investment
balances. Attached is the First Quarter Treasurer’s Report for FY24-25. The report was shared
with the City Treasurer prior to presentation to City Council.

The purpose of the report is to inform, on a quarterly basis, the City’s cash and investment
balances, the investment types, yields, and market values, and to ensure that the City’s
investments are in compliance with the City’s adopted investment policy. The report shows that
all of the City’s funds are in compliance with its investment policy. In general, operating cash is
held in US Bank checking accounts and any excess cash is invested in California’s Local
Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) and various certificates of deposit (CD5). In accordance with
Government Code sections 16429.1 and 53601 et seq., the City cannot invest more than 30%
of its portfolio in CD5. CDs accounted for 16.4% of the unrestricted cash and investments for
the quarter ended September 30, 2024.

The City reinvested one CD that matured during the quarter into a new CDs maturing in 4
years with estimated yields of 4.50%. The City takes a ladder approach with staggered
maturities for its CD investments to balance its goals of high rates in the short-term with
stability to withstand market fluctuations in the longer-term. The City will continue to assess for
opportunities to increase its investment returns while maintaining necessary liquidity and
compliance with its investment policy.

The unrestricted cash balance for the first quarter of 2024-2025 totaled $25.5 million, an
increase of $2.2 million from the first quarter of 2023-2024. The unrestricted cash balance
includes cash from enterprise funds (e.g. Harbor, Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste) not
available for general government functions. The increase in unrestricted cash is partially
attributable to the seasonality of visitor-driven tax revenues and the timing of significant capital
outlays anticipated to increase during the next fiscal year. While the majority of grant funding is
performed on a cash reimbursement basis, the unrestricted cash and investments balance
also includes $2 million in grant pre-funding received in preparation for construction of the
second phase of the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Improvement project that has not been spent as of
 September 30, 2024. The unrestricted cash balance decreased by $592 thousand compared
to the fourth quarter of 2023-2024. The decrease in unrestricted cash balance from the prior
quarter is attributable to significant capital outlays related to the Crescent Hillside Repairs
project and the completion of the Fuel Tank Replacement project. The City expects to begin
construction on several major capital projects, including the second phase of the Cabrillo Mole
Ferry Terminal rehabilitation and the Five Corners Pedestrian Improvement project, during the
next quarter which will reduce future unrestricted cash balances.

The restricted cash balance for the first quarter of 2024-2025 totaled $10.5 million, a decrease
of $1.5 million from the fourth quarter of 2023-2024. The decrease is largely attributable to the
timing of the Successor Agency’s Redevelopment Property Tax Trust Fund (RPTTF) payments
received in June to cover debt service payments of $1.6 million paid in September 2024.
Payments from the Housing Authority for capital projects at 206 East Whitley further reduced
the restricted cash balance by $236 thousand. These decreases in restricted cash balance
were partially offset by investment gains of $43 thousand in the Housing Authority’s LAIF
account, $89 thousand in the City’s landfill trust account, and increases to the CIMC
Improvement Fund of $237 thousand after disbursements for approved project costs made
during the quarter.

SUBJECT:  Authorize the Purchase of SCBA’s

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the procurement of MSA G1 Deluxe Custom Harness
packs, bottles and accessories from for a not to exceed the sum of $400,000 as budgeted in the
Fiscal Year 2024-25 Capital Improvement Plan Project Number 244501.
  -

REPORT SUMMARY: Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA) protect firefighters from
toxic fumes and smoke. They are worn on the firefighter’s back and supplies them with a fresh
breathing air source via a mask and regulator system.

SCBAs provide respitory protection for firefighters in fire suppression events including structure
and brush fires. These systems must meet standards set forth by the National Institute of
Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). NIOSH certification cycles occur every five years, and
the apparatus are not allowed to go beyond two, five-year certification cycles without the
manufacturer recertifying them.

The City’s current Honeywell Titan SCBA has been in use for over a decade and was last
certified in 2017. Additionally, Honeywell discontinued production of its SCBA product line in
2019 and has been phasing out support.

Due to factors beyond Honeywell’s control, including but not limited to increasingly limited
availability of parts and materials, the City will be submitting a request for rescission to NIOSH
for the products above, with a target of December 16, 2024. At that time, the City will no longer
be able to source support parts or repairs for these products, so they will no longer be considered
NIOSH approved and can no longer be used in occupational settings that require compliance
with OSHA Regulation 1910.134.2.

Per the City’s Purchasing Policy (Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.106(a)), Staff collected
quotes from qualified vendors MSA, Scott and Drager.
  —

  Dealer  Quote
  MSA Bauer Deluxe Model  $ 405,537.10
  MSA Curtis Deluxe Model  $ 330,926.80
  Allstar Fire Equip. SCOTT  $ 390,822.01
  Drager  $ 277,293.66
 Staff also tested each of the vendor’s products. Each vendor provided a pack and bottle to
Avalon Fire Department for an approximate month-long trial period so all members had the
opportunity to try on the apparatus and provide feedback.

The MSA Deluxe G-1 satisfies the requirement of a single piece facemask that integrates with a
USAR supplied air breathing system (SABA) and is chemical, biological, radiological and
Nuclear (CBRN), power air purifying respirator (PARP) and air-purifying respirator (APR)
certified. Additionally, the City’s partner agency, LA County Fire, also uses the MSA SC BA.

MSA is also currently running a buy one get one cylinder free until October 31, 2024. Drager is
also running that same promotion.

Though each member of the Avalon Fire Department liked the something about each packs that
were tested, the MSA package was preferred. MSA has built in TIC (thermal imaging cameras)
on each pack. This feature adds a safety feature for self-evacuation. The unit also has a reader
that the incident commander can monitor by computer to see where every firefighter is in a
building. This feature will help if they need to conduct a rescue on another firefighter.

Staff recommend the Council approve the purchase of 30 GiDeluxe MSA Custom Harness
packs, 58 45 minute Gi SCBA low profile Cylinder, with quick connect, 6 60 mm Gi SCBA
Cylinder with quick connect, up to 50 Gi Face pieces, 6 G1 Rechargeable Battery Pack, 3 quick
connect coupling, 3 Uevss 2018 Edition Gi RIT Extendaire II system, Regulator 6 ft quick fill
hose, 4 Gi SCBA Charging Station Kits, 50 Tag Assy, Electronic ID, 1 Kit Rfid Reader/Writer
Gi, and a Hub Fire Service, US which will allow the IC to see where every person is on scene
with an SCBA on.

This purchase was budgeted at $400,000 in Fiscal year 2024-2025 Project number 244501,
Account number 10225-8043.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Not aligned.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Funding for the purchase of the SCBAs is available and was budgeted with
$400,000 in Fiscal year 2024-2025 Project number 244501, Account number 10225-8043.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Avalon Fire will be out
of NIOSH and OSHA compliance for SCBA starting Jan 1, 2025

SUBJECT:  Fiscal Year 2024-2025 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule Revisions

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Hear a presentation regarding the Miscellaneous Fee
Schedule. 2. Open the Public Hearing to hear public comments. 3. Close the Public Hearing. 4.
If consensus, adopt the fee schedule as proposed.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City charges fees for miscellaneous public services, use of City
facilities and equipment rental and other activities. User fees are assessed and collected for City
services and programs provided by various departments. These are services that convey a
benefit, grant a privilege, provide for review and enforcement of regulatory activities, enforce
laws, or are a condition of development. Under State law, cities may charge fees to recoup the
direct and indirect costs related to the provision of user services.

Each year, the City reviews its fees to establish new fees, modify existing fees, and eliminate
fees that are no longer required to ensure that City fees are in-line with the costs incurred to
provide them.

On June 4, 2024, City Council approved a 3.90% increase for the majority of fees effective July
1, 2024, with the exception of transit and certain recreation fees. The percentage increase was
based on the consumer price index (CPI) information provided by the Bureau of Labor Statistics
for Los Angeles County based on the latest available fiscal year information. Using the CPI as
an average cost increase annually ensures the city does not unnecessarily burden the citizens
with unusually large spikes in fees while also ensuring that the City continues to recoup costs
associated with the increased costs to provide these services.

Since the adoption of the fee schedule, City Staff would like to propose the following new fees
to be added:

  •  Notary Fees ranging from $7.00 to $30.00 based on the services required; and
  •  Daily Temporary Residential Permit Fee of $2.00 per day

In addition, City Staff would like to propose increasing the following existing fees to better recoup
costs associated with providing these services:

  •  Tremont Hall Full Day Rental for Group 2 from $125 to $150
   •  Firefighter/Engineer from $75 per hour to $81 per hour with overtime at time and a half
  for all public safety personnel

GOAL ALIGNMENT: City costs will be offset by annual revenues.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Staff estimates that the new City fees, if adopted as proposed, would be
nominal.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The costs of special
services will not be fully funded through fees paid by the users of those services. The unfunded
portion of user services would then be subsidized by general tax revenues and/or available fund
balances.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Adopt the attached resolution establishing city rates and fees for
services.

  Scott Shapses, Deputy City Attorney, BBK

SUBJECT:  Appeal of Planning Commission Action No. 24-08 of PC#2842
  Approving a Site Plan, Conditional Use Permit, Variance and
  Coastal Development Permit at 301 Beacon Street

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Open the Public Hearing. 2. Receive Public Comment. 3.
Close the Public Hearing. 4. Consider the appeal and determine to either: a) Affirm the action of
the Planning Commission; b) Require a transcript or recording of the testimony, and all other
evidence upon which the Planning Commission made its decision, and after receiving such
evidence take such action as, in its opinion, is indicated by such evidence alone; C) Refer the
matter back to the Planning Commission, with or without instructions for further proceedings; or
d) Set the matter for hearing before itself, considered de novo. (Avalon Municipal Code (AMC)
Section 9-8.601)

REPORT SUMMARY: On August 28, 2024, the Planning Commission held a duly noticed public
hearing to consider PC#2842, a request for a Site Plan Review, Conditional Use Permit,
Variance, and Coastal Development Permit to allow demolition of a vacant three-story apartment
building and construction of a new four-story hotel with employee housing at 301 Beacon Street
(the “Project”). The property is located in the Special Commercial (SC) zone. The applicant,
Michael Flynn, represented the Project at the public hearing. The Planning Commission staff
report and meeting minutes are included as Attachments 1 and 2 of this report.

Variances were requested because the proposed Project does not comply with development
standards set forth in Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Section 9-6.304.d as follows:

  •  Allow building height of 28 feet to 44 feet, with an additional 10 feet for the elevator
  building and kitchen/restroom/mechanical roof structure, where 28 feet is allowed.

  •  Allow 97% lot coverage, where a maximum of 80% is allowed.

  •  Allow 383% floor area, where a maximum of 140% is allowed.

In the opinion of staff, the findings of fact to support the variances could be made, as there are
special circumstances related to lot topography that would otherwise deprive the property of the
development potential of other flat lots within the same zone, and the variances do not constitute
granting of special privileges and similar variances have previously been granted for the same
use on similarly sloped lots within the same zone.
After consideration of the findings in the staff report, applicant presentation, and public comment,
the Planning Commission voted 7-0 to adopt Resolution No. PC 24-08 and approve the project
 with findings and conditions as recommended by staff, with the following additional conditions of
approval (Attachment 3):

  •  The site plan and architectural plans shall be modified to provide a minimum rear setback
  of 14 feet between the building and the shared property line with 310 Metropole Avenue
  to the south of the project site.

  •  All utilities serving the project site shall be undergrounded on the property.

  •  A minimum of one hotel staff member shall be present on the roof deck at all times when
  food and beverages are being served at the roof top bar/service area.

  •  The applicant/developer shall provide a freshwater fire hydrant on the property.

  •  The applicant/developer shall coordinate with the Public Works Department to determine
  the location of, and shall be responsible for the construction of, a crosswalk as part of the
  public right-of-way improvements required to serve the Project.

On September 9, 2024, Diana Conover, owner of 310 Metropole Avenue, and Robert and Laurie
Glaser, owners of 314 Metropole Avenue, filed a timely appeal of the Planning Commission’s
decision, requesting that the City Council review the Planning Commission’s approval of the
Project. The appeal application details concerns regarding the granting of the height variance,
potential impact of views from adjacent properties on Metropole Avenue to the coast and
surrounding hillsides, potential for increased traffic and noise in the area due to the planned
rooftop bar and restaurant, and the amount of parking provided on the Project site relative to
parking demand of the area. The complete appeal application is included asAttachment4, which
provides the appellant’s written factual and legal claims regarding the proposed Project. Below
are the assertions made by appellant Conover and are followed by staff response.

First Assertion  —  Special Variances

“The proposed development deviates significantly from the allowable Development Standards
in the SC Zone, particularly in terms of height limitations, lot coverage, and floor area. For
instance, the Development Standards in the SC Zone allow a height limit of 28 feet, while the
development proposes a height of 28 to 44 feet to the top of the parapet, with an additional 10
feet for a rooftop elevator kitchen/restroom enclosure. This proposal adds 16 to 26 feet over the
allowable height limit, which greatly affects the views and enjoyment of neighboring properties.”

Staff Response:

Staff observes that, of the three variances from the development standards that the Planning
Commission approved, only the variance for building height appears to be challenged the
appellant. The approved variances as to lot coverage and floor area have not been disputed by
the appellant, the appellant only indicates that there is deviation from development standards,
the purpose of a variance. Accordingly, while it does not appear that the variances as to lot
coverage and floor area are at issue, this section discusses the basis for issuance of those
variances as well.

Variances from development standards may be permitted when the findings in AMC Chapter 9-
8.405 are made, and Resolution No. PC 24-08 included all variance findings required by the
code. While there is deviation from the development standards in the SC Zone, a variance is the
 legal mechanism to allow such deviations “when, because of special circumstances applicable
to the property including size, shape, topography, location or surroundings, the strict application
of the Zoning Ordinance deprives such property of privileges enjoyed by other property in the
vicinity and under identical zoning classification.” (AMC Section 9-8.405) (emphasis added)

The proposed Project is on a lot with sloped topography, which differs from the topography of
other similarly situated lots. Most lots in the Special Commercial (SC) zone are located in the
area commonly known as the “Flats.” Those lots typically have a flat topography that lends itself
to the maximum building height in the SC zone, 28 feet. Under the AMC, building height means
  the vertical distance from the lot’s natural surface to the highest point of the building.” (AMC
Section 9-608) (emphasis added) In other areas of the City, which have steep hillsides, it was
recognized that appropriate adjustments to maximum building height would need to be made in
order to account for the differences in slope on those lots. Strict application of the zoning
standards in the SC zone for this property, which has an unusually sloped lot for the area, would
mean that the buildable area of the lot would be substantially less than that of a flat lot. This
would deprive the property of the same development potential as compared to other properties
within the same zone. Additionally, staff also notes that this property has sat vacant for decades.
Its vacancy provides some circumstantial evidence that the development potential of the lot may
have been, in part, one reason that the property had not been developed sooner.

Moreover, by way of comparison, other properties with hotels on sloped lots within the immediate
vicinity of the Project have been approved with variances as to height, floor area, and lot
coverage for the zone. Records approving these projects did so on the basis of the topography
of the lots, recognizing that exceeding the permitted development standards was further
supported by the fact that those properties fit within the context of the existing development and
topography of the surrounding area.

Staff therefore reiterates its conclusion in the Planning Commission staff report that the proposed
variances conform with the required municipal code variance findings given the special
topography of the lots, and because no special privileges will be granted to the applicant that
differ from those previously granted for the same use on similarly sloped lots within the same
zone. The appeal on the ground that the height variance was inappropriate should be denied.

Second Assertion  —  Impact on Views

“The proposed development threatens to obstruct and eliminate the mountain and coastline
views from 314 Metropole Ave., 310 Metropole Ave., and neighboring properties. This would not
only diminish the enjoyment of these scenic vistas but also significantly decrease the rental and
property values. The impact on the residents of 310 and 314 Metropole Aye, who include several
local families working on the island, is particularly concerning. They have invested in their homes
and their views, and the proposed development undermines their hard-earned right to enjoy their
surroundings.”

Staff Response:

The Planning Commission may consider impacts to views as part of its decision to approve
PC2842, however, it is not the sole basis under the AMC on a decision whether or not to grant
an application, Impacts to views was considered by the Planning Commission. The second
required finding for the Conditional Use Permit, under AMC Section 9-8.404(a)(2), discusses
that the applicant intentionally placed the accessory restaurant/mechanical building on the
rooftop in a location that was intended to minimize potential impacts to views of adjacent
 buildings to the harbor. In the fourth required finding for the Variance, under AMC Section 9-
8.405, it is discussed that the Project is located over 800 feet from the mean high tide line of
Avalon Bay and that the site is not adjacent to and does not provide direct or indirect visual or
physical access to, the shoreline of Avalon Bay, coastal hillsides or bluffs, or other significant
viewsheds identified in the Avalon Local Coastal Plan. This consideration was taken into
account by the Planning Commission when it approved the height. Similarly, in the first findings
for the Coastal Development Permit, it was observed that the Project complies with Section
30250 of the Coastal Act because the Project is located within the urban center of Avalon, on a
developed parcel surrounded by other commercial, institutional, and residential uses, and is not
located in a position that impedes a designated coastal viewshed on the Avalon Local Coastal
Plan. While the Planning Commission may consider “adverse effects on neighboring property,”
impacts on property values of adjacent properties is not a factor that the Planning Commission
considers when deciding on the entitlements requested under PC2842. Instead, the Planning
Commission should find that it is possible to “prevent adverse effects on neighboring property,”
and found the applicant was able to prevent such effects for the reasons specified in the Planning
Commission staff report, resolution, and for the reasons expressed above.

Thus, the Planning Commission fully considered impacts on views when approving PC2842 and
the City Council should reject impacts on views as a basis for granting the appeal.

Third Assertion  —  Increased Noise and Traffic

“The proposed development is likely to increase noise levels and traffic congestion in the area.
Construction activities will inevitably generate significant noise, disrupting the tranquility of the
neighborhood. Additionally, the design of the development includes a rooftop bar and restaurant
area that will contribute to increased noise levels from gatherings and other activities, further
disturbing the peaceful environment of the neighborhood. Once completed, the new
development will attract additional traffic, further straining the already limited roadways and
exacerbating the current traffic issues. This increase in noise and traffic will negatively impact
the quality of life for nearby residents and diminish the overall appeal of the area.”

Staff Response:

The Planning Commission considered noise impacts and traffic congestion as part of its approval
of PC2842. In the second finding for the approval of the Site Plan Review, under AMC Section
9-8.203(b), the findings discuss that the rooftop bar and restaurant area will be open from 7:00
AM until 10:00 PM daily. The applicant would be required to apply for a Special Event Permit if
conducting activities or uses different from ordinary food service operations. The applicant is
also required to comply with all applicable requirements of the Noise Ordinance for Noise District
3 under AMC Section 5-1 3.08. In the second finding of approval for the Conditional Use Permit,
under AMC Section 9-8.404(a)(2), the Planning Commission considered that there would not be
an adverse impact to noise due to the need for compliance with the Noise Ordinance.
Additionally, technical studies were prepared to analyze potential impacts of the proposed
Project on traffic, noise, and air quality. The studies concluded that the project would not
generate a significant number of new vehicle trips, increase ambient noise levels by more than
2 decibels, or generate construction or operations related to emissions beyond thresholds set
by the South Coast Air Quality Management District. Further, Condition 6 of the Conditions of
Approval requires that the operation of the hotel comply with AMC Chapter 9-13 Noise and states
that the operator shall not use or operate or cause to be used or operated outdoors any sound
amplifying equipment, among other similar listed prohibited activities, that would make sound
plainly audible from the real property line unless permitted with a Special Use Permit.
 Construction between the hours of 7:00 pm and 8:00 am is disallowed by Condition 7 of the
Conditions of Approval. The Planning Commission staff report also discusses that the roof deck
is surrounded by a glass railing along the parapet wall, and the rooftop kitchen and mechanical
equipment building is placed to provide separation between the roof deck and adjacent
residential uses to the east and south. The Noise Impact Analysis prepared for the Project was
attached to the Planning Commission staff report as Appendix B of Attachment 6. Even at
maximum capacity of 100 estimated persons, and with mechanical equipment operating, the
analysis concluded noise levels would be increased by no more than 2 decibels beyond ambient
noise levels, an increase that is imperceptible to ordinary persons.

 Impacts to traffic were similarly addressed in the Planning Commission staff report. The operator
will provide a commercial autoette to transport those arriving from the docks to the hotel. The
applicant has been required to provide a designated parking space for the commercial autoette,
as well as an adjacent loading zone. This will significantly mitigate impacts from commercial
vehicles, preventing the blocking of traffic along Metropole Avenue. This same requirement
imposed on the applicant was considered in both findings three and four for the Conditional Use
Permit, under AMC Section 9-8.404, where it was found and determined that the site will be
adequate in size and shape to accommodate parking and loading facilities to properly integrate
into the neighborhood. Specifically, the operation of the business would not interfere with
circulation at the corner of Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street because the applicant will
provide designated parking for the commercial autoette, as well as adjacent loading and drop
off zones. Further, the primary use of the property will be transitory housing, where guests will
predominantly be dropped off by rideshare vehicles or other transport vehicles, minimizing an
increased to vehicles operated on the island relative to residential uses. The second finding for
approval of the Site Plan Review, under AMC Section 9-8.203, similarly finds that the designated
parking and loading areas and use of the site for transitory stays will sufficiently mitigate traffic
impacts sufficiently to avoid traffic congestion and preserve the public health, safety, and general
welfare and prevent adverse effects on neighboring property. The technical study referenced
and incorporated into the Planning Commission staff report as Appendix B of Attachment 6
analyzed traffic impacts and concluded that there would not be significant effects to traffic from
the Project.

Thus, the Planning Commission fully considered impacts on noise and traffic when approving
PC2842.

The possibility that four additional autoettes may be parked on the street, if applied for by the
resident employees, will be considered in the subsequent staff response to concerns regarding
parking.

Fourth Assertion  —  Lack of Parking

“The development plans indicate insufficient on-site parking for an area that is already struggling
with parking shortages. This could exacerbate the existing parking issues for residents and
visitors alike, further straining the community’s resources.”

Staff Response:

Parking was devoted its own entire section in the Planning Commission staff report. It is found,
as above, that the applicant will provide an on-site autoette and designated parking space for
that autoette that will act as a ride sharing vehicle, limiting significantly parking impacts. The
autoette will be parked in a covered parking space at the southwest corner of the building, where
 that autoette will have ready access to Metropole Avenue. The hotel operator will use an existing
stiped loading zone on Metropole for commercial deliveries, and a new 3-minute loading zone
will be added at the entrance of the hotel. That loading period will allow for rapid circulation of
traffic at the entrance, preventing overflow impacts to adjacent roadways. That loading zone will
also act as a stop for the Avalon COAST transit system, encouraging the use of public transit
thereby minimizing the number of vehicles that would be required to park on the adjacent streets.

It is possible, that four employee housing units could qualify for residential autoette permits, if
the nine-month residency requirement in the code is satisfied. However, this number of added
permits is insignificant to the total number of autoette permits issued for the area and will not
produce a significant impact where there is sufficient parking available for an additional four
added permits. The fact that most parking will be done for limited periods, only to drop-off visitors
to the hotel, and planned operation of a commercial autoette for drop-offs, demonstrates that
there will be minimal aggregate impacts to parking. Those features of the project were
considered in finding three and four of the Conditional Use Permit, under AMC Section 9-
8.404(a)(3)(4), noting that the use of the commercial autoette and adjacent loading and drop-off
zones would minimize parking impacts. Similarly, finding two of the Site Plan Review, under
AMC Section 9-8.203(b) observed that parking impacts would be significantly curtailed by the
use of the designated parking for the commercial autoette in combination with the mitigation
provided by the adjacent loading and drop-off zones.

Thus, the Planning Commission fully considered impacts on parking when approving PC2842.

Fifth Assertion  —  Review of Commission Decisions

“The Planning Commission agreed to changes to the application at the meeting but did not
require Mr. Flynn to provide updated plans for further review. We believe this is a serious
misstep, as it prevents a thorough understanding of how these changes will impact the project.
Mr. Flynn offered several hypothetical scenarios regarding the potential impacts of these
changes but did not provide any concrete details. Kelly specifically advised that adding updated
plans as a condition would be prudent, but her advice was disregarded.

Additionally, Mr. Flynn categorically denied planning to include a bar and restaurant open to the
public, with a 100-person capacity and operating hours from 7AM to 10 PM. He asserted
that the space would be for hotel guests to gather and relax. If this is indeed his intention, then
the “bar and restaurant” terminology currently in the application should be removed to avoid
any confusion about what will actually be allowed on the deck.”

Staff Response:

Applications are commonly approved with added conditions or modifications to the original
project design, and those modifications are subject to review and approval by staff. It is not the
Planning Commissions role to approve the plans submitted by an applicant, instead, that is the
role of the Planning and Building Department. Mr. Flynn has provided revised conceptual plans
for staff review, included as Attachment 5 of this report. As reviewed, the conceptual plans

  DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS

Issue 1: Variances from Development Standards

The applicant is requesting multiple variances from the development standards for the SC zone, as
follows:

  •  Allow building height of 28 feet to 44 feet, with an additional 10 feet for the elevator
  building and kitchen/restroom/mechanical roof structure, where 28 feet is allowed.
  •  Allow 97% lot coverage, where a maximum of 80% is allowed.
  •  Allow 383% floor area, where a maximum of 140% is allowed.

Per AMC Chapter 9-8.405, variances from development standards may be permitted by the
Planning Commission where the special circumstances may deprive a property of privileges
enjoyed by other property in the vicinity and under identical zoning classification, the property is
not granted special privileges beyond those available to similar properties, does not permit a use
that is otherwise not allowed, and complies with the Avalon Local Coastal Program.

Though the property is of regular size, the sloped topography of the lot is unusual compared to the
majority of other properties within the SC zone. The majority of lots within the Special
Commercial zone, and commercial zoning districts in general, are located within the “Flats”. As a
result, the development standards have been written to apply to lots with flat topography. For
instance, the maximum building height in the SC zone is 28 feet. The municipal code definition
for building height is “…the vertical distance from the lot's natural surface to the highest point of

  6
65059.00002\42583158.2
 the building.” (AMC Section 9-3.608). Other zones in the city, particularly the residential zones,
have additional detailed standards for measurement of building height (low slope, hillside, steep
hillside) that account for the topography present within the zone to allow for equitable
development of all lots. However, in the case of a sloped lot in the SC zone strict application of
the definition of building height would mean that the actual buildable area of the lot would be
substantially less on a sloped lot than a flat lot, which would deprive the property of the same
development potential compared to other properties within the same zone.

The requested variances are consistent with approved development of other properties with hotels
on sloped lots within the immediate vicinity of the project. The Hotel St. Lauren (231 Beacon
Street) and Casa Maraquita (229 Metropole Avenue) are hotel projects also developed in the SC
zone under the same development standards which exceed development standards, including
height, floor area, and lot coverage standards for the zone. According to the permitting records for
these projects, approval was granted because of the topography of the lots, and with
acknowledgement that while the hotels were larger than permitted by the development standards
for the zone, they fit within the context of the existing development and topography in the
surrounding area.

Therefore, it is the opinion of staff that the proposed variances may be granted in conformance
with the findings of the municipal code, as there are special circumstances related to lot topography
that would otherwise deprive the property of the development potential of other flat lots within the
same zone, and the variances do not constitute granting of special privileges and similar variances
have previously been granted for the same use on similarly sloped lots within the same zone.

Issue 2: Employee Housing

AMC Section 9-11.104.d requires that any new commercial development shall provide rental
housing for at least 50% of the peak season employees. The applicant has estimated that four full-
time employees will be employed by the business with the completion of both phases of the project.
The proposed project shall provide housing for four employees, consisting of one manager suite
and three housekeeper studio units on-site, which exceeds the housing requirements of the
municipal code.

There is no standard unit size requirement for employee housing units. However, all rentals must
be for the period of not less than six months to provide for housing stability for employees. Rents
for such accommodations may be established by the hotel operator with City approval.

The proposed project is subject to audit by the City following the first peak season after
commercial operations have commenced to ensure that a sufficient amount of employee housing
has been provided to accommodate at least 50% of peak season employees. The City reserves the
right to modify the new commercial development's rental space requirements in line with
municipal code requirements if the estimation in this application is deficient.

 Issue 3: Parking

The applicant proposes to provide on-site autoette parking space for the project. This space is to
be designated for parking of a commercial autoette to service the hotel. The vehicle will be parked
in a covered parking space at the southwest corner of the building, with access to Metropole
Avenue. An existing striped loading zone on Metropole Avenue will be maintained to facilitate
commercial deliveries, and a new 3-minute loading zone is proposed to be added at the entrance
of the hotel on Beacon Street, as shown on the site plan in Attachment 3. The Beacon Street
loading zone may also serve as a designated stop for the Avalon COAST transit system.

The four employee housing units may qualify for residential autoette permits, subject to the
municipal code residency requirements for residential autoette permits. Resident employees will
not have access to the parking space reserved for the commercial autoette.

Per AMC Section 9-6.304, the number off-street parking spaces required for a development may
be determined by the Planning Commission as part of the review of the project application. The
Planning Commission may consider factors such as operational characteristics, site layout, and
surrounding development when considering approval of off-street parking.

It is the opinion of staff that the proposed parking plan can be found sufficient for the proposed
hotel operation. The primary use of the property will be transitory housing and guests are
anticipated to be dropped off by a rideshare (such as a taxi or other transport vehicle) at the curb
at Beacon Street where they would enter the hotel lobby. This will prevent interference with
circulation at the corner of Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street, which is a heavily used
intersection. Designated parking for the commercial autoette, combined with the adjacent loading
zone, will ensure that commercial vehicles do not block traffic along Metropole Avenue, which is
functionally narrow due to on-street parking on both sides of the street.

It is possible that up to four additional autoettes could be parked on the street, if resident employees
meet the 9+ month residency requirement for a residential autoette permit, which is not guaranteed.
However, this is a small number of vehicles compared to the overall number of autoettes permitted
within the city and is not anticipated to have a substantial impact on the available on-street parking
within the “Flats” and surrounding areas.

Issue 4: Rooftop Deck Operations

According to the applicant, the rooftop deck will be a gathering place for hotel guests to sit and
enjoy the views of Avalon Bay and the surrounding hillsides. The rooftop deck is designed with a
600 SF building that is a combination prep kitchen/bar/restroom where hotel guests can purchase
beverages (including alcohol) and light food, such as tapas, salads and appetizers. The rooftop
deck food and beverage service will also be open to the public. The rooftop deck will be open from
7:00 AM until 10:00 PM. Weddings and other events may be held on the rooftop deck, however,
each event will be required to apply for a Special Event Permit (AMC Chapter 4-6) and
demonstrate compliance with all city code requirements.

  8
65059.00002\42583158.2
 Use of the rooftop deck has the potential to create noise nuisance for surrounding properties.
Operations must be consistent with Avalon Municipal Code Section 5-13.08 for a building within
Noise District 3, which states that it is “unlawful to use or operate or cause to be used or operated
outdoors any radio receiving set, sound amplifying equipment, television set, or other machine or
device which produces or reproduces sound in such a manner as to be plainly audible from the real
property line on which the sound amplifying equipment is located unless permitted by Special Use
Permit.” The applicant is not requesting approval of a Special Use Permit at this time.

It is the opinion of staff that with limited hours of operation and the requirement for a Special
Event Permit for events, the proposed roof deck is compatible with the intent of the SC zone and
should not cause undue noise nuisance to surrounding properties. The roof deck is surrounded by
a glass railing along the parapet wall, and the rooftop kitchen and mechanical equipment building
is placed to provide separation between the deck and adjacent residential uses to the east and south.
This conclusion is further supported by the Noise Impact Analysis prepared for the project,
provided as Appendix B of Attachment 6 of this report. The analysis concluded that with the roof
at maximum capacity (estimated 100 people), and with rooftop mechanical equipment operating,
the proposed project will increase noise levels by no more than 2 decibels over existing ambient
noise levels, which will not be a perceptible increase in general loudness to the human ear.

  ENVIRONMENTAL DETERMINATION

California Environmental Quality Act:

The proposed project is categorically exempt from the provisions of the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines 15332 (Class 32 – In-fill Development Projects)
because it has no potential to have a significant effect on the environment.

The Class 32 reflects a determination by the California Office of Planning and Research (OPR)
that projects that meet the Class 32 criteria will not have a significant environmental effect and,
therefore, are exempt from CEQA. (Berkeley Hillside Preservation v. City of Berkeley (2015) 60
Cal.4th 1086, 1102.) To apply, a project must be an in-fill development and meet the following
criteria: (1) is consistent with the applicable General Plan designation and applicable policies, as
well as applicable zoning designations and regulations, (2) would occur on a site less than five (5)
acres, (3) the project site must have no habitat value, (4) the project would not result in significant
traffic, noise, air quality, or water quality effects, and (5) the site can be adequately served by all
required utilities and public services. The Class 32 exemption reflects the understanding that “the
majority of private projects for which a government permit or similar entitlement is necessary are

  17
65059.00002\42583158.2
 minor in scope … and hence, in the absence of unusual circumstances, have little or no effect on
the public environment.” (Pacific Palisades Residents Association, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles
(2023) 88 Cal.App.5th 1338, 1363.) If a project meets the criteria and qualifies for the Class 32
exemption, the project is categorically exempt from CEQA unless one of the exceptions to
exemptions apply. The exemption is not limited to any use type and may apply to residential,
commercial, industrial, public facility, and/or mixed-use projects.

The project meets all of the aforementioned requirements and is exempt under Class 32, as
supported by substantial evidence:

  a) General Plan and Zoning Consistency: The project site is designated Special Commercial
  (SC) by the General Plan Land Use Element and is located within the SC Zoning District.
  The SC designation provides an area in which both small scale residents and neighborhood

  the SC with approval of a Conditional Use Permit.
  b) Less Than 5 Acres: The project site is approximately 3,225 square feet (0.07 acres), which
  is less than five acres.
  c) No Habitat Value: The project site is located in an urban area currently developed with an
  three-story apartment building. Because of the existing site’s developed nature in a highly
  urban environment the site has no value as habitat for endangered, rare, or threatened
  species. There is no sensitive vegetation or habitat on-site. The project would not encroach
  into any jurisdictional waters or areas that support native and/or sensitive habitat. The
  property does not contain any wetland areas.
  d) No Significant Traffic, Noise, Air Quality or Water Quality Effects: Technical studies have

SECTION 2 – ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

The proposed project is categorically exempt from the provisions of the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines 15332 (Class 32 – In-fill Development Projects)
because it has no potential to have a significant effect on the environment.

The Class 32 reflects a determination by the California Office of Planning and Research (OPR)
that projects that meet the Class 32 criteria will not have a significant environmental effect and,
therefore, are exempt from CEQA. (Berkeley Hillside Preservation v. City of Berkeley (2015) 60
Cal.4th 1086, 1102.) To apply, a project must be an in-fill development and meet the following
criteria: (1) is consistent with the applicable General Plan designation and applicable policies, as
well as applicable zoning designations and regulations, (2) would occur on a site less than five (5)
acres, (3) the project site must have no habitat value, (4) the project would not result in significant
traffic, noise, air quality, or water quality effects, and (5) the site can be adequately served by all
required utilities and public services. The Class 32 exemption reflects the understanding that “the
majority of private projects for which a government permit or similar entitlement is necessary are
minor in scope … and hence, in the absence of unusual circumstances, have little or no effect on
the public environment.” (Pacific Palisades Residents Association, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles
(2023) 88 Cal.App.5th 1338, 1363.) If a project meets the criteria and qualifies for the Class 32
exemption, the project is categorically exempt from CEQA unless one of the exceptions to
exemptions apply. The exemption is not limited to any use type and may apply to residential,
commercial, industrial, public facility, and/or mixed-use projects.

The project meets all of the aforementioned requirements and is exempt under Class 32, as
supported by substantial evidence:

  a) General Plan and Zoning Consistency: The project site is designated Special Commercial
  (SC) by the General Plan Land Use Element and is located within the SC Zoning District.
  The SC designation provides an area in which both small scale residents and neighborhood
  retail and services can coexist harmoniously. Hotels and residential uses are permitted in
  the SC with approval of a Conditional Use Permit.
  b) Less Than 5 Acres: The project site is approximately 3,225 square feet (0.07 acres), which
  is less than five acres.
  c) No Habitat Value: The project site is located in an urban area currently developed with an
  three-story apartment building. Because of the existing site’s developed nature in a highly
  urban environment the site has no value as habitat for endangered, rare, or threatened
  species. There is no sensitive vegetation or habitat on-site. The project would not encroach

  10
   into any jurisdictional waters or areas that support native and/or sensitive habitat. The
  property does not contain any wetland areas.
  d) No Significant Traffic, Noise, Air Quality or Water Quality Effects: Technical studies have
  been prepared that analyze the potential impacts of the proposed project on the surrounding
  community related to traffic, noise, and air quality. These studies conclude that the project
  will not generate a significant number of new vehicle trips, increase the ambient noise
  levels by more than 2 decibels, or generate construction or operations related emissions
  beyond the thresholds adopted by the South Coast Air Quality Management District. The
  site is currently fully developed, and a non-priority Water Quality Management Plan will
  be required to be prepared at the time of grading permit review.
  e) Utilities and Public Services: All required utilities, including sewer, water, energy, are
  existing within the project site. Southern California Edison has issued a water allocation
  for Phase 1 of the project, for up to 10 bedrooms/units. All public services, including police
  and fire protection, are adequate to accommodate the project. As conditioned and designed,
  the project will be adequately served by all required utilities and public services

Furthermore, the project was evaluated pursuant to the criteria for the exceptions to the exemptions
as identified in Guidelines Section 14 CCR, Chapter 3, Article 19, Section 15300.2 and found that
there are no exceptions to the use of an exemption for the project. The Property does not impact
an environmental resource of hazardous or critical concern, does not result in cumulative impacts,
does not have a significant effect on the environment due to unusual circumstances, does not
damage scenic resources within a state scenic highway, is not a hazardous waste site, and is not
identified as a historical resource. Therefore, no further analysis is required. A Notice of
Exemption will be filed with the County of Los Angeles Clerk of the Board.

  2  PROJECT OVERVIEW

2.1  Introduction

Pursuant to Section 15367 of the State CEQA Guidelines, the City of Avalon (City) is the public agency that
has the principal responsibility for conducting or approving a project.

Applicant Hamilton Pacific, LLC, Inc proposes to demolish the existing vacant building on APN 7480-031-
040, which is a 3,325 SF lot on the southeast corner of Beacon Street and Metropole Avenue and construct
a hotel. The Proposed Project would demolish the existing, vacant, 5,882 square foot (SF) three-story
residential building that is up to 44 feet high (northeast building corner) and contains 10 units and
construct a new 12,212 SF four-story hotel at a maximum height of 28 feet at the parapet (southwest
building corner), that would include 37 hotel rooms, four hotel employee studio units and a rooftop deck
that includes accessory structures of an elevator and combination outdoor prep kitchen/bathroom
structure that would provide light food and beverage service where the accessory structures would
extend approximately 10 feet above the parapet.

Demolition of the existing building would occur with labor and hand power tools, and no heavy equipment
would be utilized except to prepare the building pad for final grading once the building demolition has
been completed. Interior room completion would be completed in two phases, based on water allocations
by Southern California Edison which dictates development in the City based its operation of the City’s
water system. Operations consist of that for a typical hotel. The Project Site is zoned as Special Commercial
(SC).

The City, as the lead agency for the Proposed Project, is responsible for preparing environmental
documentation in accordance with CEQA to determine if approval of the discretionary actions requested
and subsequent development of the Proposed Project would have a significant impact on the
environment. As such, this document is designed to meet the requirements for the City of Avalon’s
Environmental Assessment/CEQA compliance.

2.2  Background

Applicant Hamilton Pacific, LLC offers full service general contracting services throughout Southern
California. The Applicant is also currently the developer and contractor for the Hamilton Cove
Development in Avalon, and currently has approximately 15 to 30 construction employees working on
any given day depending on the work activity. The Applicant currently houses employees during the week
in a combination of hotels and other transient housing. Given the housing shortage in the City of Avalon
and the Hamilton Cove development is anticipated to continue for another five to 10 years, the Applicant
has chosen to lease and redevelop the existing building at 301 Beacon Street for the purpose of providing
a more permanent solution to the long-term temporary housing needs of its Hamilton Cove construction
employees and develop/operate a hotel to off-set the costs of the building development. It is anticipated
that housing his employees in this development would free up approximately 10 to 20 rooms in hotels
and in other transient housing in Avalon.

The building at 301 Beacon Street has been vacant for more than 20 years, is in a state of disrepair, and
has become somewhat of an eyesore in a prominent area of the City. A structural evaluation of the
building conducted by the applicant has determined that remodeling or renovating the building is not
feasible, and it must be completely demolished and reconstructed.

Therefore, the Applicant is proposing to demolish the building and reconstruct it to current standards. All
of the 37 hotel rooms range from 200 to 230 SF, which is greater than the 190 SF as required by Avalon
Municipal Code Section 9-7.901, and the bathrooms average 50 SF, which is greater than the 35 SF
required by the City code. An additional four studio apartments are provided for the hotel manager and
housekeeping staff.

Once completed, the Applicant would contract with the hotel operator for exclusive rights to use three to
four hotel rooms during the weekdays for the Hamilton Cove construction workers, who are currently
housed in various transient housing and hotels throughout the City. These rooms would be released for
visitors and/or other workforce housing on the weekends.

The Applicant has identified that the benefits of this Project to the City include the following:

  •  Additional transient occupancy taxes for 37 hotel rooms;

  •  Additional availability of hotel rooms for visitors;

  •  Create four to five new jobs for administration and other duties, with four jobs offering live-in
  accommodations as hotel workforce housing.

2.3  Project Setting and Location

The proposed Project is located at the southeast corner of Beacon Street and Metropole Avenue in the
City of Avalon and is identified as 301 Beacon Street, Los Angeles County Assessor Parcel No. (APN) 7480-
031-040. Refer to Figure 1: Regional Vicinity and Figure 2: Project Location located at the end of this
section.

The Project site is within the USGS 7.5’ quadrangle Santa Catalina East, within Topographic Quad
Coordinates: Township 9 South, Range 14 West, Latitude: 33°20'33.46" N / Longitude: 118°19'41.80" W.

2.3.1  Existing Conditions

The building and Proposed Project is situated on the southeast corner of Metropole Avenue and Beacon
Street.

The Project Site is vacant 5,882 SF three-story, 22-foot-high building that contains 10 residential units. The
existing building footprint occupies approximately 2,859 SF of the 3,325 SF lot, with an approximately 466
SF patio, which represents an approximately 19-foot-wide setback.

The three-story building was constructed in 1923, designed in a vernacular style with elements of
Mediterranean Revival. The building includes two shallow wings that project from the east and south
corners. The building has a flat roof that has a centralized stepped parapet at the northwest elevation.
The stepped parapet meets in the center of the northwest elevation and includes a tower-like projection
with a hipped roof that is approximately 34 feet tall. The main roof is rolled asphalt, and the tower
projection structure is clad with shingles. The building is wood frame construction, sheathed in non-
original vinyl siding.

It was constructed with some units existing below the street grade, which allows the roofline to remain
flat, similar to the neighboring buildings along Metropole Avenue which also have units below street grade
due to the street’s steep slope. Therefore, the above-ground elevation of the building is shorter along the
rear of the building at Metropole Avenue than it is along the frontage at Metropole Avenue and Beacon
Street. The existing building height is 22 feet at the rear of the property.

There are recessed ground-level entrances at all four elevations, framed by archways and accessed by
concrete steps with original wood landings. All doors except one are wooden with multi-pane glazing. The
northeast elevation contains recessed entrances framed by archways that lead to a metal fire escape on
the upper levels. The entrance on the southwest elevation is surrounded by a metal canopy. Fenestration
appears to be original consisting of double-hung, one over wood frame windows with lambs tongue
details. The first-floor windows on all elevations are covered with wooden lattices.

There is one Pepper tree at the rear of the building. There is no other vegetation, or habitat for sensitive
species.

The existing building housed short-term and seasonal visitors after its construction in 1923 and was also
occupied by the property owner’s family between approximately 1930 and 2000. However, it has been
vacant since approximately 2000 and has fallen into a state of disrepair. The building does not meet
current building code standards and significant termite damage is present.

2.4  Project Description

Applicant Hamilton Pacific, LLC, Inc proposes to demolish the existing vacant building on APN 7480-031-
040, which is a 3,325 SF lot on the southeast corner of Beacon Street and Metropole Avenue (a cross-
sloped lot) and construct a hotel. The Proposed Project would demolish the existing, vacant, 5,882 square
foot (SF) three-story residential building that is 22 feet high (southwest building corner) and contains 10
units and construct a new 12,212 SF four-story hotel at a maximum height of 44 feet at the parapet
(northeast building corner), that would include 37 hotel rooms, four hotel employee studio units and a
rooftop deck with an elevator (80 SF) and a bathroom and outdoor prep kitchen accessory structures
(total 480 SF) that would extend approximately 10 feet above the parapet.

The existing building has been determined to be in an extremely deteriorated state, structurally deficient,
and demolition is required. Demolition of the existing building would occur with labor and hand power
tools only, and no heavy equipment would be utilized except to prepare the building pad for final grading
once the building demolition has been completed.

Operations consist of use of typical hotel operations. Once completed, the Applicant would contract with
the hotel management for exclusive rights to use three to four hotel rooms during the week for his
Hamilton Cove construction crew, and these rooms would be available to visitors and other workforce
housing on the weekends.

2.4.2  Construction Characteristics

Initial site improvements include demolition, grading and underground infrastructure followed by building
construction and painting activities. Site grading would be limited to minor removal and soil balancing
with little to no import or export of fill material. Project construction would require the use of heavy
equipment such as one backhoe, concrete trucks, and a water truck.

It is anticipated that the entire property boundary would be fenced and screened.

All construction would occur in accordance with City guidelines, Section 5-13.06, which makes
construction within 500 feet of residential zones, hotels, or motels unlawful between the hours of 7:00
p.m. and 8:00 a.m. or at any time on Sundays.

Construction Phasing

The Project would be developed in two phases based on the SCE water allotments for the property. In
accordance with SCE water allotment guidelines, the Project can currently only occupy rooms that make
up a total of 10 water units until SCE develops additional capital improvements, the schedule of which is
unknown at this time, but is anticipated to be near the end of 2025. With these capital improvements in
place, SCE would be able to serve water to the additional 34 units, or a total of 44 water units for the hotel
rooms. Additional water credits from SCE to operate the roof-top restaurant would be required prior to
operation.

The following construction phasing is anticipated, although may change, based on the water credits issued
by SCE.

Phase 1 is anticipated to occur between September 2024 and January 2026 (10 total water units), but may
vary depending on construction crew scheduling:

  •  Demolition, final grading, utilities as needed.
  •  Build the hotel infrastructure, exterior/architectural, install elevator to all four floors with rooftop
  access, all mechanical to fully support first phase.
  •  Develop first floor interior that would contain lobby, seven private, double-occupancy hotel rooms,
  and one manager’s apartment, (8 water units). All hotel rooms in this phase would be designed for
  two persons per room, in accordance with SCE water allotment standards.
  •  Develop second floor interior with 1 of the 10 planned hotel rooms and 1 housekeeper suite (2
  water units).
  •  Develop third and fourth floors to rough-in only with fire sprinklers.

It is the intent that the facilities and rooms developed during Phase 1 would be occupied upon completion
of Phase 1.

2.4.4  Best Management Practices Prior To and During Construction

The applicant is required to follow all existing regulations during construction that serve to avoid and/or
minimize potential impacts. In addition to compliance with all federal, State and Local codes and
ordinances, the applicant would incorporate several industry-standard best management practices in the
construction specifications to avoid potential impacts to environmental resources. The City would also
include the applicant-proposed measures as Conditions of Approval. These include but are not limited to
the following:

  •  South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD) Compliance. The applicant is required
  to comply with various rules and regulations from the SCAQMD, including but not limited to the
  following:

  o  SCAQMD Rule 402: Prohibits a person from discharging from any source whatsoever such
  quantities of air contaminants or other material which cause injury, detriment, nuisance, or
  annoyance to any considerable number of persons or to the public, or which endanger the
  comfort, repose, health or safety of any such persons or the public, or which cause, or have a
  natural tendency to cause, injury or damage to business or property.

  o  SCAQMD Rule 403: Governs emissions of fugitive dust during construction and operation
  activities. Compliance with this rule is achieved through application of standard Best
  Management Practices, such as application of water or chemical stabilizers to disturbed soils,
  covering haul vehicles, restricting vehicle speeds on unpaved roads to 15 miles per hour,
  sweeping loose dirt from paved site access roadways, cessation of construction activity when
  winds exceed 25 mph, and establishing a permanent ground cover on finished sites.

  o  SCAQMD Rule 481: Applies to all spray painting and spray coating operations and equipment.

  o  SCAQMD Rule 1113: Governs the sale, use, and manufacturing of architectural coating and
  limits the VOC content in paints and paint solvents. This rule regulates the VOC content of
  paints available during construction. Therefore, all paints and solvents used during
  construction and operation of the project must comply with SCAQMD Rule 1113.

  o  SCAQMD Rule 1143: Governs the manufacture, sale, and use of paint thinners and solvents
  used in thinning of coating materials, cleaning of coating application equipment, and other
  solvent cleaning operations by limiting their VOC content. This rule regulates the VOC content
  of solvents used during construction. Solvents used during the construction phase must
  comply with this rule.

  o  SCAQMD Rule 1403: Asbestos Emissions from Demolition/Renovation Activities, specifies
  work practice requirements to limit asbestos emissions from building demolition and
  renovation activities, including the removal and associated disturbance of asbestos-
  containing materials (ACM).

  •  Payment of Developer Impact Fees (DIF). The Project is subject to payment of a development
  impact fee (DIF) which is intended to construct or acquire needed facilities, preserve open space,
  and habitat needed to serve new developments as well as transportation facilities including roads,
  bridges, and traffic signals.

  •  Migratory Bird Treaty Act Compliance/Pre-Construction Nesting Bird Surveys. Bird nesting
  season generally extends from February 1 through September 15 in southern California and
  specifically, April 15 through August 31 for migratory passerine birds. To avoid impacts to nesting
  birds (common and special status) during the nesting season, a qualified Avian Biologist will
  conduct pre‐construction Nesting Bird Surveys (NBS) prior to project‐related disturbance to
  nestable vegetation and trees to identify any active nests. If no active nests are found, no further
  action will be required. If an active nest is found, the biologist will set appropriate no‐work buffers
  around the nest which will be based upon the nesting species, its sensitivity to disturbance,
  nesting stage and expected types, intensity and duration of disturbance. The nests and buffer
  zones shall be field checked weekly by a qualified biological monitor. The approved no‐work
  buffer zone shall be clearly marked in the field, within which no disturbance activity shall
  commence until the qualified biologist has determined the young birds have successfully fledged
  and the nest is inactive.

  •  Construction Noise Good Neighbor Practices. To further ensure that construction activities do
  not disrupt the adjacent land uses, the following best management practices would be followed
  during construction:

  1. Construction to occur in accordance with the City of Avalon’s Noise Ordinance which allows
