assessed the impact of a pending addition to the property’s historic fabric.
1051 Marine Drive, Historic Resource Assessment and Impacts, Laguna Beach, CA. Architectural Historian. Valerie
provided research and updated an existing impact assessment for a 1920s Beach Cottage with a Craftsman-influenced
style in Laguna Beach. Valerie evaluated the property using the new Laguna Beach Historic Preservation Ordinance and
assessed the impact of a pending addition to the property’s historic fabric.
Columbia University, The Harlem Renaissance: Preservation, Spatial Encounter, and Anti-Racism, Harlem, NY.
Architectural Historian/Student. As a graduate student, Valerie contributed to a group research report that examined the
legacy of the Harlem Renaissance, its significance in anti-Black racism histories and its place-based associations. This
included an in-depth study of the era, Harlem as the Black mecca, and the exploration of preservation through an
innovative community lens. The goal of the report was to instrumentalize the heritage of the Harlem Renaissance toward
anti-racism and social justice while also identifying and preserving key assets for the Black community.

graduate student, Valerie contributed to a group conservation project that examined the layers of paint in the historic

Dear City Clerk Gabrielle Morones and Avalon California City Council,

We, the property owners of 314 Metropole Ave. and 310 Metropole Ave., as residents and
frequent visitors to Avalon, wish to appeal the recent Planning Commission vote regarding the
proposed development at 301 Beacon St. We have reviewed Application # PC2842 and have
several concerns that we would like to bring to your attention:

Special Variances: The proposed development deviates significantly from the allowable
Development Standards in the SC Zone, particularly in terms of height limitations, lot
coverage, and floor area. For instance, the Development Standards in the SC Zone allow a
height limit of 28 feet, while the development proposes a height of 28 to 44 feet to the top of
the parapet, with an additional 10 feet for a rooftop elevator kitchen/restroom enclosure. This
proposal adds 16 to 26 feet over the allowable height limit, which greatly affects the views and
enjoyment of neighboring properties.

Impact on Views: The proposed development threatens to obstruct and eliminate the
mountain and coastline views from 314 Metropole Ave., 310 Metropole Ave., and neighboring
properties. This would not only diminish the enjoyment of these scenic vistas but also
significantly decrease the rental and property values. The impact on the residents of 310 and
314 Metropole Ave, who include several local families working on the island, is particularly
concerning. They have invested in their homes and their views, and the proposed development
undermines their hard-earned right to enjoy their surroundings.

Increased Noise and Traffic: The proposed development is likely to increase noise levels and
traffic congestion in the area. Construction activities will inevitably generate significant noise,
disrupting the tranquility of the neighborhood. Additionally, the design of the development
 includes a rooftop bar and restaurant area that will contribute to increased noise levels from
gatherings and other activities, further disturbing the peaceful environment of the
neighborhood. Once completed, the new development will attract additional traffic, further
straining the already limited roadways and exacerbating the current traffic issues. This
increase in noise and traffic will negatively impact the quality of life for nearby residents and
diminish the overall appeal of the area.

Lack of Parking: The development plans indicate insufficient on-site parking for an area that
is already struggling with parking shortages. This could exacerbate the existing parking issues
for residents and visitors alike, further straining the community's resources.

Review of Commission Decisions: The Planning Commission agreed to changes to the
application at the meeting but did not require Mr. Flynn to provide updated plans for further
review. We believe this is a serious misstep, as it prevents a thorough understanding of how
these changes will impact the project. Mr. Flynn offered several hypothetical scenarios
regarding the potential impacts of these changes but did not provide any concrete details.
Kelly specifically advised that adding updated plans as a condition would be prudent, but her
advice was disregarded.

Additionally, Mr. Flynn categorically denied planning to include a bar and restaurant open to
the public, with a 100-person capacity and operating hours from 7 AM to 10 PM. He asserted
that the space would be for hotel guests to gather and relax. If this is indeed his intention, then
the "bar and restaurant" terminology currently in the application should be removed to avoid
any confusion about what will actually be allowed on the deck.

We respectfully request that these concerns be carefully considered.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. The check for the appeal, as well as a hard copy of
the appeal letter has been mailed.

SUBJECT:  Coyote Joe’s Outdoor Patio Lease Assignment

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the assignment of the lease for city-owned real
property at 113 Catalina Avenue from Seabring Inc., dba Coyote Joe’s Restaurant to Coyote
Joe’s Bar and Restaurant, LLC.

REPORT SUMMARY: On September 23, 2024, City Staff received a request from Ron Bevins,
representing Seabring, Inc., dba Coyote Joe’s Restaurant, to assign the remaining term of his
lease with the City of Avalon for exterior space at 113 Catalina Avenue to Martin Leyva, dba
Coyote Joe’s Bar and Restaurant, LLC.

The exterior space, comprised of approximately 418 square feet, is currently used for outdoor
dining. Per the lease agreement, any assignment must be approved by the City Council.

Additionally:
  -  The lease establishes a base rate of $3.25 per square foot (CPI adjusted annually).
  Currently, the lease rate is approximately $3.90 per square foot or $1,629.80 a month.
  -  The property may only be used for tables and chairs and similar furnishings to
  accommodate food and beverage sales and consumption and for no other purpose
  whatsoever.
  -  The property is required to be open nine (9) months each year.
  -  The initial term of the lease is through December 31, 2025 with one, five year renewal
  term.

City Staff recommend the City Council authorizes assignment of the lease maintaining all of
the existing lease terms on the following conditions:
  1. The sale of the business is finalized.
  2. Confirmation of the Catalina Island Company’s approval of the assignment.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Lease revenue.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The tenant will be
required to remove tables from the public right-of-way and honor the area outlined within the
original lease agreement.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: Pursuant to the Brown Act.

SUBJECT:  Cabrillo Mole Rehabilitation Phase II Pre-Construction Stage 0

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Hear a presentation regarding Construction Stage 0 of Phase
II of the Cabrillo Mole Rehabilitation Project. 2. Authorize the implementation of Stage 0 of the
Cabrillo Mole Rehabilitation Project including approval of the Cabrillo Mole Temporary Facility
Plan, four step procurement process, administrative procedure for existing tenants at the Cabrillo
Mole, and approval of the site plan. 3. Make the affirmative finding that the City has made its
best effort to relocate the tenants at the Cabrillo Mole, and suitable facilities for the Catalina
Island Company’s ticket booth, Island Enterprises’ ticket booth and storage area, Catalina ATM,
Inc., and Fish Feeder business cannot be accommodated. 4. Delegate authority to the City
Manager to negotiate and execute reasonable rent agreements with tenants that will be
relocated to temporary facilities during construction including the Avalon Blue Line Baggage,
Catalina Express, Catalina Passenger Services (Flyer), and Eli’s Island Deli.

REPORT SUMMARY: The Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal is a multimodal transportation hub used
by cross-channel carrier passengers traveling between the City and the mainland, cruise ship
disembarkmentlembarkment, and serves as the primary entry point to the City. In 2020, the City
completed Phase 1 of the Cabrillo Mole Rehabilitation Project which included the rehabilitation
and reinforcement of the existing concrete members, replacement of the steel grates, and
repaired the concrete deck and railing for a total project cost of $5.10 million.
  —

The next portion of the project, budgeted at $20 million, will replace and reconfigure the existing
building and structures to improve passenger queuing and adjacent transportation circulation.

In order to accommodate sustained, mostly uninterrupted operations of the Cabrillo Mole,
construction of the new facility has been broken into 10 construction stages. The Pre
Construction Stage Stage 0 Includes the following four steps:
  —  —

1. Installation of grates at the old steamer ramp ways along the easterly face of the Mole
  wharf.
  This portion of the project will be implemented by a competitive procurement as outlined in
  Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.106(d). The City will solicit a request for bids (RFB) from
  qualified contractors to install grates over the top of two existing cut outs along the easterly
  face of the Mole. These grates will allow construction and emergency vehicles an
  approximate twenty-foot pathway so they may access the full length of the mole throughout
  the construction project. The grates will become a permanent addition to the mole wharf. In
   addition, the southern portion of the mole wharf (last two grates near the crane) was
  scheduled to originally be completed during the Phase 1 project; however, due to funding
  and timing constraints, mainly associated with COVID-1 9, the work was not completed. After
  bids are received, the final contract will be brought back to City Council for final approval.

2. Installation of utility systems and other temporary infrastructure to support the future
  Cabrillo Mole facility as well as temporary facilities.
  This portion of the project will be implemented by a competitive procurement as outlined in
  Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.106(d) and as previously authorized by the City Council
  on December 12, 2023. The scope of work associated with this bid will include installation of
  upgraded utility systems to support the new facility as well as utilities to support temporary
  facilities that will be used during the construction project. The contractor will also raise the
  planter areas adjacent to Floats 4 and Floats 5 and install decking to provide a space for
  queuing for commercial businesses relocated to the roadway during construction. After bids
  are received, the final contract will be brought back to City Council for final approval.

3. Purchase of long-lead equipment associated with the upgraded utility system.
  This portion of the project will be implemented by a competitive procurement as outlined in
  Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.106 (a). Staff will solicit via posted notice, telephone
  request, mail, email or fax, price quotes for equipment necessary for the utility systems, but
  may have more than 12 month lead time, including the electrical switching gear. After quotes
  are received, the procurement authorization will be brought back to City Council for final
  approval.

4. Purchase temporary facilities.
  This portion of the project will be implemented by a competitive procurement as outlined in
  Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.106 (a). Staff will solicit via posted notice, telephone
  request, mail, email or fax, price quotes for lease or purchase of office containers to house
  commercial entities during construction, as well as restroom facilities. Staff anticipate
  procurement of one 40” container, two 20’ containers, and one 10’ container, in addition to
  stand alone restroom facilities. After quotes are received, the procurement authorization will
  be brought back to City Council for final approval.

All businesses at the Cabrillo Mole will be impacted by the construction project. City Staff
developed the Cabrillo Mole Temporary Facility Plan to allow for the relocation of the most
essential services in order to preserve the highest level of operation for the duration of the
project.

Currently there are 11 lessees at the Cabrillo Mole:
  • Avalon Blue Line Baggage  •  Catalina Island Company
  • Catalina ATM, Inc.  •  Island Enterprises
  • Catalina Passenger Services (Flyer)  •  Gregory Wenger dba Fish Feeder
  • Catalina Express  •  Assorted Antennas (3)
  • Eli’s Island Deli

Per the City’s leases with the current tenants at the Cabrillo Mole:
   Mole Renovation. Lessor will use its best efforts to relocate Lessee’s business during
  renovations of the Mole if such renovations render the Property unfit for the operation of
  Lessee’s business. Lessor makes no guarantees regarding the size, location, fitness or
  availability of any temporary alternative premises. Upon completion of the Mole
  renovations, lessees affected by the renovations will have first right of refusal to reopen
  their businesses in renovated space on the Mole. In the event Lessor is unable to locate
  suitable alternative temporary space for Lessee’s business during the Mole renovation,
  Lessee hereby releases Lessor from all liability related to the same, as further described
  in Paragraph 14 of this Lease.

The space available for temporary facilities is small  accounting for a cumulative total of
  —

approximately 720 square feet. Temporary facilities will be placed within the street at the tops of
Floats 4 and 5. As described in Step 4, the adjacent planter area will be raised with decking
installed to provide space for queuing. The temporary facilities will be container boxes minimally
outfitted with drywall finishes, flooring, HVAC systems, and electrical and internet hook ups.

While developing a temporary facility plan for the relocation of tenants, City Staff prioritized
essential services passenger transport, restroom facilities, baggage handling, etc. Additionally,
  —

Staff considered if the operator had redundant locations within Avalon. In balancing the needs
of the public and emergency services, the proposed temporary facility plan will relocate the
Catalina Express, Catalina Flyer, Eli’s Island Deli and Avalon Blue Line Baggage. Staff have
identified these as essential services directly related to operations at the Cabrillo Mole.

Though Staff have made its best effort to identify an appropriate location for the other tenants at
the Cabrillo Mole, a suitable location cannot be identified. Three of the commercial businesses
that will not be relocated have additional operation facilities in Avalon  the Catalina Island
  —

Company and Island Enterprise businesses have ticketing facilities on the Pleasure Pier, Fish
Feeder has additional feeding stations on the Pleasure Pier as well as along Lover’s Cove.

As outlined in the lease agreements, all tenants, including those not provided a temporary facility
location, will be offered first right of refusal for space within the new Cabrillo Mole facility.

City Staff recommend the City Council delegates authority to the City Manager to negotiate and
execute reasonable rent agreements with tenants that will be relocated to temporary facilities
during construction including the Avalon Blue Line Baggage, Catalina Express, Catalina
Passenger Services (Flyer), and Eli’s Island Deli. Staff anticipate these temporary leases will
only be in place for approximately 2 years.

If approved, City Staff will begin negotiating new leases with tenants that will be relocated, taking
into consideration capital outlays that may be needed for tenant improvements in the temporary
facilities as well as the new facility. Additionally, Staff will inform tenants that will not be relocated
of the timeline for construction and of their options under the current lease agreements.

To minimize the impact to businesses and visitors during the summer, Staff hope to complete

SUBJECT:  Options for City Council in Considering Tenant Protection and Rent
  Control Measures

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Consider and discuss tenant protections and rent control
options available under State law, and provide direction to City of Avalon (“City”) staff to
evaluate and report back on any desired local options available to the City.

REPORT SUMMARY: The purpose of this staff report is to provide the City Council with
information on State law as it relates to tenant protections and rent control, and provide
examples of what other cities have codified locally so the City Council may consider what
policy options it is interested in exploring for Avalon.

  City of Avalon’s Municipal Code and Existing Tenant Protections
The City currently has no specific provisions in the Avalon Municipal Code (“AMC”) that impose
City-created rent control (also known as “rent stabilization”). Chapter 9-1 1 of the AMC includes
City-specific Affordable Housing requirements. The purpose of Chapter 9-1 1 is meant to
“[e]ncourage the availability of dignified, safe, and affordable workforce housing within the City
of Avalon by promoting development of decent living environments and removing unnecessary
barriers to such development.” (AMC 9-11.101(c).) This includes a City inclusionary housing
requirement to construct a percentage of affordable housing as part of any new residential
development. Specifically, for any new residential development creating five or more for-sale or
rental units, developers are required to set aside at least 20% of those units at an affordable
rent or cost (pursuant to State income limits). However, these City requirements are only
applicable to new commercial or residential development, and do not provide tenant protections
or affordability controls for existing housing stock.

  II.  State Law: The Tenant Protection Act of 2019 and Its Subsequent Changes

A.  2019 Framework, the Tenant Protection Act
In 2019, the State Legislature approved and the Governor signed Assembly Bill 1482, the
Tenant Protection Act (the “Act”). The Act set the “floor” with a series of new tenant protection
measures that must be followed by all California landlords. However, cities can go above that
“floor” in setting more protective local controls for its tenants.

The Act broadly prevents landlords from terminating or declining to renew leases with tenants
of at least a year without “just cause,” as defined under California Civil Code section 1946.2.
 “Just cause” is divided into two categories, “no-fault” termination and “at-fault” termination,
which each have their own eligibility criteria and protections for tenants. The information below
is meant to provide a non-exhaustive summary of the provisions under the Act. Importantly,
when a landlord evicts a tenant under no-fault just cause, the landlord must pay relocation
assistance equal to one-month’s rent, regardless of tenant income1. As described in additional
detail below, a number of cities have required more significant relocation benefits than one-
month, and expanded the types of evictions eligible for relocation benefits.

  •  No-Fault Termination: includes but is not limited to, withdrawal of the unit from the
  rental market; or an intent to demolish or “substantially remodel” the residential
  property.
  a The definition of a “substantial remodel” that qualifies as a no-fault termination
  includes:
  when the remodel “cannot be reasonably accomplished in a safe manner”
  with the tenant present, and requires the tenant to vacate for at least 30
  consecutive days, and either:
  • (1) replacement or substantial modification of any structural,
  electrical, plumbing, or mechanical system that requires a permit; or
  • (2) the abatement of hazardous materials.

  •  At-Fault Termination: includes but is not limited to, instances where tenant is in default
  on rent; breach of any material term of the lease (generally after landlord issues a
  written notice to correct); and a nuisance as defined under State law (including unlawful
  possession of weapons and the manufacture, cultivation, or possession for sale of
  controlled substances).

The Act also includes a statewide “floor” of rent control. Specifically, State law limits rent
increases over a 12-month period, with a maximum increase of no more than 5% plus the
percentage change in the Consumer Price Index (“CPI”), or 10% percent, whichever is
lower.

It is important to note there are a series of exemptions from the applicability of the Act written
into State law. The following reflects a non-exhaustive list of housing types that are not subject
to State law tenant protections, which include: affordable housing restricted by deed or subject
to existing rent or price controls; dormitories; single-family, owner-occupied residences;
housing less than 15 years old; and some mobile homes.

B.  State Law Amendments Strengthening the Act (SB 567)

Senate Bill 567, which became operative on April 1, 2024, tightened the rules for no-fault just
cause evictions, substantial remodels and rent increases. SB 567 created stricter enforcement
rules to reduce the ability of landlords to evict tenants and then rent out the unit at market rate.

1 To  be eligible, a tenant must have continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months or
more.
 For an eviction by the landlord because the landlord or their family member will be moving into
a dwelling unit with an existing tenant (a type of no-fault just cause eviction), the landlord or
family member must not already live on the property or have access to another vacant unit on
the property. The landlord or family member also must move in within 90 days of the tenant
moving out, and stay in the unit for at least a year. Tenants have the right to know the
relationship of any family member who is moving in, and can request proof. A vacating tenant
is also given the opportunity to move back in at the same rent rate, along with moving
expenses, if the landlord or family member does not move in within the specified timeframe or
fails to stay for the full year.

For substantial remodels, landlords must provide a detailed notice outlining the work to be
done, any necessary permits, and inform tenants that they can return to their units if the work
is not completed or if they do not need to vacate during certain days.

Regarding the Act’s rent control provisions, SB 567 introduced penalties for landlords who
collect rent above the maximum allowed, based on the rent amount that was overcharged, that
may also include attorneys’ fees and court costs. A landlord may also be penalized up to three
times the amount of charged rent, if they acted willfully or with malice. They may also be liable
for damages. These new laws did not change the existing law on rent control or
allowable rent increases under the Act.

It is important to note that as a general rule, the State-adopted Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing
Act (“Costa-Hawkins”) limits the extent to which cities and counties can enact rent control or
rent stabilization ordinances. Specifically, the City of Avalon could only adopt a rent control
measure that applied to apartments (excluding single family homes and/or condominiums) that
received their certificate of occupancy before February 1, 1995. Costa Hawkins allows only
the owner/landlord (and not local government) to set the rental rates for units that received
certificates of occupancy after February 1, 19952. Additionally, cities and counties can
legislate only on rental increases, and may not set the initial rental rate. For those reasons,
in all the cities and counties with rent control ordinances that are described below, any time a
tenant voluntarily moves out, the landlord is permitted to set the new rent without restriction,
based on the new tenancy.

On November 5th 2024, California voters will consider Proposition 33, which would eliminate
Costa-Hawkins and give cities and counties more rent control authority while also preventing
the State from taking future actions that limit local rent control.3

C.  New California Laws with Additional Tenant Protections
There are two, additional new laws aimed at improving housing security and protecting tenants
from unfair evictions and rent increases that are described briefly below.

  •  AB 12: Limits the security deposit landlords can collect to a maximum of one
  month’s rent. An exception is made for “small property” owners (those with no

2See California Civil Code section 1954.52.
 The California Legislative Analyst’s Office’s nonpartisan Proposition 33 analysis can be located at:
https:/IlaocaqovIBallotArys/PrQppsWon?nurnber=33&year=2O24.
   more than two properties and a total of four or fewer units), who may still collect
  up to two months’ rent.

  •  AB 1418: Prevents local governments from adopting regulations that encourage
  evicting tenants based on calls to law enforcement, alleged criminal activity, or
  other alleged nuisances. AB 1418 also prohibits local governments from requiring
  or encouraging landlords to conduct criminal background checks when screening
  tenants.

  Ill. Examples of Tenant Protection and Rent Control Actions Taken by Other Cities

The City Council may provide direction to codify requirements set out under State law so
Avalon may take local, administrative enforcement action, including issuing administrative
citations that include City approved penalty amounts, or adding local civil or criminal remedies.
The City Council may also provide direction for City staff to evaluate  —for possible future
review and adoption more protective local tenant protection and rent control actions. Below
  —

are examples of what a number of other cities have done, that can serve as a reference point
for what may be of interest to Avalon.

A majority of the cities cited below are charter cities. Charter cities have greater authority to
govern themselves than a general law city, like Avalon. However, and as described above, the
Tenant Protection Act and related State laws provide the “floor,” not the ceiling. State law
allows local tenant protection and/or rent control ordinances so long as they provide the same
or better protections for tenants, with corresponding findings that the local ordinance is both
consistent and “more protective” than State law. This is true for both charter cities and general
law cities.

Accordingly, should Council provide direction to evaluate rent control in the City of Avalon, the
City’s ordinance can be more protective than the “floor” set out under the Act, should ensure a
process by which landlords can petition (appeal) the City to increase the otherwise allowable
rent increase for a fair return of investment, and finally, upon direction, our office will ensure
the proposed local ordinance is otherwise consistent and not preempted by any State or
Federal law (including Costa-Hawkins) or any law after the voters vote on Proposition 33. Any
adopted ordinance should also evidence the City’s interest in promoting long-term stability and
certainty for renters, in addition to any other Avalon-specific public purposes.

Whatever direction the City Council provides, City staff will work with the City Attorney’s Office
to ensure any proposed policy change on tenant protections and/or rent control that come back
to the City Council are vetted consistent with State law.

A.  Examples of Locally-adopted Rent ControllRent Stabilization Ordinances

  •  Culver City. Culver City has adopted a series of more expansive rent control and
  tenant protections than under State law. For relocation assistance, Culver City requires
  a relocation fee to be the greater of three times the tenant’s current monthly rent or an
 amount established U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”)
formula that is based on fair market rent.

Culver City does not allow no-fault just cause eviction when the tenant is 62 years or
older, is disabled or terminally ill, is a qualifying low-income tenant under State income
limits, or when the tenant has school-aged children who are protected from eviction
during the school year term.

Culver City caps annual rent increases at no more than 5% annually. However, if the
percentage change to the consumer price index (“CPI”) on an annual basis is less than
2%, rent increases in Culver City may not exceed 2% that year. If CPI is greater than
5%, the annual 5% cap still applies and no increase may exceed that percentage.
There are exemptions, including but not limited to, when State or Federal law expressly
exempts the unit from price control and when the landlord receives government
subsidies for the unit. Importantly, Culver City’s rent control measures apply only to
otherwise eligible units that received their certificate of occupancy before February 1,
1995. This threshold date is within local rent control measures, since it is controlled
under State law (see discussion above on Costa-Hawkins).

Similar to other cities and regulations discussed in additional detail below, landlords
may petition the city if they believe the rent control regulations prevent them from
earning a fair return on their property investment.

For no-fault terminations, such as property demolition or when a landlord or their
relative is moving in, Culver City requires landlords to pay relocation assistance. This
amount is typically three times the monthly rent plus an additional $1,000. Small
landlords, defined as those owning three or fewer units, are required to pay less.
Landlords can deduct any past due rent from the relocation payment.

Landlords in Culver City must also register their rental units annually with the city, and
pay an annual fee per rental unit. Culver City’s annual fee is established by City
Council resolution, meant to recover the City’s reasonable costs managing the program
(similar to other cities with annual registration fees, described below). A penalty is
imposed for late registration, and Culver City has enforcement mechanisms in place to
ensure compliance. This includes issuing administrative citations with fines of up to
$1,000 per day. Culver City may also bring civil actions against landlords who violate
these regulations.

County of Los Angeles. The County of Los Angeles imposed rent control on units in
unincorporated areas of the county via an ordinance in 2018, and have been expanding
and refining its codified provisions since that time. The County’s Department of
Consumer and Business Affairs (“County Department”) is responsible for the calculation
of the annual, allowable rent increase, for evaluating landlord petitions seeking a higher
increase based on a fair return of investment theory, and also runs the County registry.
The County Department promulgates the necessary procedures and guidelines for how
the program is run.
   The County of Los Angeles has rent control limits for qualifying rental units, and
  separately for “luxury units” as defined. A “luxury unit” has 2-bedrooms or less, is
  located in a complex with at least 25 dwelling units, and, as of September 11, 2018,
  charges more than $4,000 per month in rent. Over calendar year 2023, an annual rent
  increase was limited to 5% for luxury units. Currently, the annual rent increase shall not
  exceed 10% for luxury units, though the County Department retains the ability to amend
  that percentage in the future.

  Only one rent increase is allowed over a 12-month period, and any rent paid in excess
  of the local ordinance must be reimbursed to the tenant. Units subject to the county’s
  rent control are required to be within buildings with two or more units, and for the
  reasons discussed above, must have received their Certificate of Occupancy (or
  equivalent) on or before February 1, 1995.

  For all non-”luxury units” subject to rent control, the formula is calculated by the County
  Department annually based on the following evaluation of the Consumer Price Index
  (“CPI”) for the Los Angeles-Riverside-Orange County, California area:

  o  1. If the change in CPI is eight percent (8%) or higher, the maximum allowable
  annual rent increase will be eight percent (8%);
  o  2. If the change in CPI is between three percent (3%) and eight percent (8%), the
  maximum allowable annual rent increase will be equal to the change in CPI;
  o  3. If the change in CPI is between one percent (1 %) and three percent (3%), the
  maximum allowable annual rent increase will be equal to three percent (3%);
  o  4. If the change in CPI is between negative two percent (-2%) and one percent
  (1%), the maximum allowable annual rent increase will be equal to the change in
  CPI plus two percent (2%); and
  o  5. If the change in CPI is less than negative two percent (-2%), no annual rent
  increase is permitted.

  However, for calendar year 2024, the county’s ordinance limits the maximum
  allowable rent increase permitted to 4%. Additionally, the Board of Supervisors, by a
  3-2 vote this past June, provided additional direction for staff to evaluate a more tenant-
  protective rent cap of 3% for qualifying rental unit, with 4% permitted for smaller
  property owners, and 5% for luxury units4.

  Landlords may file an application with the County Department if they do not believe they
  are receiving a fair and reasonable return on their investment based on the allowable
  rent increase. The Los Angeles County Code includes a rebuttal presumption that the
  rent increase is fair and reasonable, and the landlord has the burden to prove the
  necessity of any additional rent increase to earn a fair and reasonable return. The
  county evaluates a number of factors to determine whether the landlord has proven the

   burden to increase rent above the set formula, including but not limited to: rental history;
  changes in property taxes; improvements made to the rental property and its overall
  physical condition; and decreases in net operating income. The landlord must provide
  notice to its tenant(s) when they file a request with the county to increase above the

  A landlord must register each rental unit with the county annually, and the county may

  •  Santa Ana. Beginning in 2021, Santa Ana limited annual rent increases to no more
  than 3% of the current rent, or 80% of the change in the Consumer Price Index,

  Santa Ana included findings within its adopted ordinance that a CPI-based increase

  Santa Ana does allow a landlord to submit a petition to the Rent Stabilization Program

  excess of what is otherwise allowed. In evaluating a petition, the Program Administrator
  appoints an impartial hearing officer, who looks to many of the same factors utilized in
  other jurisdictions (rental history; changes in property taxes; the need for repairs, etc.).
  In addition, a Santa Ana hearing officer may evaluate changes in utility charges,
  reasonable operating expenses, and compare the rent lawfully charged to comparable
  rental units in the City of Santa Ana in making their determination.

  Landlords may also submit a “Capital Improvement Petition” to the Program
  Administrator seeking a pass-through of certain costs to tenants to construct capital
  improvements in the unit. Such capital improvements include but are not limited to
  structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanism systems; roofing; carpeting; and air

   conditioning systems. Santa Ana requires that pass-through costs must be calculated
  by looking at the amortization over the useful life of the improvement, but in no instance

  •  Ojai. The City of Ojai’s ordinance limits annual rent increases to 4%, which the City
  finds provides a just and reasonable return on a landlord’s property, and includes the

  Sacramento, similar to other jurisdictions, sets the annual tenant protection program

B.  Examples of Other Tenant Protections, Adopted Locally:

  •  Long Beach. The City of Long Beach offers increased relocation payments for any
  tenants displaced due to City’s code enforcement activities; for instance, when the
  Building Official issues a notice to vacate for necessary repairs of the unit. Finding that
  low income tenants were most at risk of being displaced for substantial repairs,
  remodels or demolition, Long Beach requires relocation benefits in the amount of
  $3,366.00 per household, with additional payments due when the tenant is disabled.
  Additionally, Long Beach imposes a penalty, in an amount not to exceed $10,000, for
  failure to make timely, required relocation payments on a specific property with a
  displaced tenant.
   •  Pasadena. Pasadena includes heightened relocation benefits for tenants that are in
  “good standing” (generally meaning the tenant is not in breach of their rental
  agreement) in households at or below 140% of the median income. In that instance,
  landlords are required to provide two and half months in fair market rents as established
  by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”), for a rental unit of
  a similar size. Pasadena also requires landlords pay a $1,306.00 moving expense for
  adult households, or $3,935.00 for households with dependents, disabled, or senior
  members6. There are exceptions from these relocation requirements for single family
  homes and condominium units.

  Pasadena also offers temporary relocation benefits if a landlord is required to
  temporarily (less than 120 days) recover possession of a rental unit. In those instances,
  the tenant should be paid an amount based on a daily rate equal to two (2) times the
  daily pro-rata portion of the rental rate. The landlord must also pay actual costs
  associated with moving and storage.

FISCAL IMPACTS: None.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will still follow
the requirements of State law, including the Tenant Protection Act, and its existing Municipal
Code requirements, but will not provide direction to explore additional tenant protections.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: That the City Council provide City staff with direction regarding what, if
any, tenant protections and/or rent control measures that are permissible under State law
should be explored for the City of Avalon. Any follow-up would return to City Council for future
consideration and possible codification.

 SUBJECT:  Presentation and Discussion on Landlord Tenant Regulatory Options

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Consider existing landlord tenant regulations under state law,
as well as City options for creating additional regulations, and direct Staff to prepare a tenant-
landlord ordinance for future consideration if the Council deems it appropriate.

REPORT SUMMARY: State law provides certain landlord tenant regulations throughout the
state, but cities may enact additional regulations if they so choose. The report summarizes
current state regulations and discussions other regulations cities have enacted.

California’s Tenant Protections

California’s Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (‘TPA”) prevents a landlord from evicting tenants
without ‘just cause,” Just cause may be “at-fault” or “no-fault.” At-fault just cause allows the
landlord to evict and provide little to no assistance. But no-fault just cause requires the landlord
to provide assistance to the evicted renter (even though the landlord still gets to evict).1

A (-fault
“At-fault” just causes include: default in payment of rent, breach of a material term, nuisance,
waste, refusal to sign a new lease, criminal activity, unauthorized assignment or subletting,
refusing entry to landlord, using the property for an unlawful purpose, and termination of
employment if employee housing.

No-fault
“No-fault” just causes include: use of the unit by the owner’s family; withdrawal of the unit from
the rentai market; a court or other government order to vacate the property; and “intent to
demolish or to substantially remodel” the unit, With no-fault just cause, the landlord must pay
relocation assistance equal to one month rent, regardless of tenant income.

Exemptions
The TPA does not apply to a short-term rental or hotel; housing for a nonprofit hospital, religious
facility, or various care facilities; school dorms; owner-occupied housing (sharing kitchen or
bathroom with owner); single-family owner-occupied residences; an owner-occupied duplex;
housing built within the last 15 years (except for mobile homes); housing that is separately

Floor, not ceiling.
The TPA sets the floor for new tenant protections; it does not prevent a city from adopting
additional protections.

The TPA does not apply to properties that are subject to a local ordinance that requires just
cause for termination if the local ordinance was adopted before September 2019. (I.e., if the ocal
ordinance predates September 2019 and it has a just-cause requirement, it prevails over the
TPA even if the TPA is more strict.)

Nor does the TPA apply to properties that are subject to a newer local ordinance (post-
September 2019)  as long as the ordinance is at least as protective as the TPA
  —

Summarizing the TPA
The statewide TPA provides some benefits (one-month’s rent for relocation) in some situations
(specific enumerated no-fault evictions). It does not prevent eviction. It allows eviction for a major
remodel. And it doesn’t apply to several types of housing.

Avalon has no local tenant-protection ordinance, so any ordinance that it might adopt must be
at least as protective as the TPA.

Options for Additional Local Protections

Many California cities adopt local regulations to provide additional protections for renters. These
additional protections tend to be the following:
  • Eliminating or narrowing certain just causes (e.g., not allowing “major remodel” as a no-
  fault just cause).
  • Increasing relocation assistance (e.g., three or four months’ worth of rent).
  • Expanding the protections to other types of dwellings (e.g., eliminating exemption for
  newer homes).
  • Imposing rent control.
  • Create rent registry and rent-control board to consider exceptions to rent-control
  restrictions.
Require minimum lease periods (e.g., one-year mm initially).

The Council may consider these and other options for providing additional tenant protections as
long as they are at least as protective as the TPA.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Only those tenant
protections that are imposed by state and county laws and regulations will apply.
